newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania's bank privatisation is urgent, president says.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania's bank privatisation is urgent, president says.

text.p: Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa has urged his parliament to ratify legislation covering the sale of the country's biggest state-owned commercial bank before the end of the month.

Addressing a parliamentary committee of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party on Saturday in Dodoma, central Tanzania, Mkapa said it was "urgent and necessary" to privatise the National Bank of Commerce (NBC), the state-owned Sunday News reported.
"If the bank is not privatised soon the people will have to pay 19 billion shillings ($30 million) annually in taxes to support it for the next 10 years," he said.
The current budget session of Tanzania's National Assembly, sitting in Dodoma, runs until August 29.
Last month Mkapa said the NBC would be split into two separate operations -- a trade and regional bank, and a micro-finance bank.
Experts from the World Bank had recommended the NBC be split into three independent operations.
The World Bank, irritated at the slow pace of the bank's privatisation, is withholding payment of $125 million in Structural Adjustment Credit (SAC) until the restructuring begins.
Privatisation of the ailing bank has blown up into Tanzania's biggest domestic political controversy.

The NBC was founded in 1967 under the sweeping socialist economic policies introduced by then president Julius Nyerere. It operated as a monopoly until 1992 when foreign commercial banks were licensed in western-backed economic reforms.

Nyerere, Tanzania's founding father now retired from the presidency, has fueled the controversy by expressing concern that privatisation of the bank he founded could deny the impoverished rural community access to credit facilities.
His critics said his concern was unrealistic because the NBC was too cash-strapped to offer credit and its inefficiency was a national embarrassment.

Mkapa told CCM MPs that efforts by the government to prop up the bank -- including a cash injection of 43 billion shillings, retrenchment of 3,000 workers and the closing of 20 branches -- had not worked.
Mkapa said the government would retain a 30 percent equity in both new banks. These shares would be offered for sale to the public at a later date.
But the majority shareholding would be offered for sale to a strategic investor with enough experience and capital to run the bank.
